description: We are building a survival map for Mars
summary:
Crimson Exodus converts NASA Mars data into an interactive browser game as the form of Interplanetary Survival Guide. The player prepares a Marswalk in Jezero Crater with the help of the real site map made of NASA’s Perseverance elevation data, a mineral layer from CRISM, and the actual path taken by Perseverance. The player takes the walk in 3D environment as an astronaut named Jack, accompanied by a robot that can interact with the player. The player operates scientific stations, monitors the depletion of oxygen, energy, water, and CO2 scrubber resources, as well as dust storms and solar flares calibrated according to NASA data collected on Mars. The base on Earth is 11 light-minutes away, calculated live in real-time; therefore, mission control cannot respond on time, and player must make own decisions about turning back.

The importance: all images of Mars exploration that have been seen by the public were generated by a rover, and a rover is able to sit still while waiting for instructions from Earth. Humans are not. Crimson Exodus brings the true limitations of a human on a distant planet in ways that are understandable to students and the general public.
details:
A playable Mars EVA planning and field-science simulation, built on NASA open data.

It runs in any web browser, with nothing to install.

▶ Play it here, and try the two-minute demo from the title screen.

The problem

Every image of Mars exploration that anyone on the earth has seen was captured using a rover, which can just sit and wait for Earth; astronauts cannot. The difficult part about an astronaut exploring Mars is the time period after they open the hatch because he/she will have to rely on a limited backpack, a limited sol, unexplored terrain, unpredictable weather, and mission control that is 21 minutes away.

How it works: three stages

1. Plan your path based on actual NASA data: In Jezero Crater, you have to pick from three possible paths to three science stations, each based on an actual site that was investigated by Perseverance: Kodiak butte, Hogwallow Flats, and the Séítah surface. The planner calculates oxygen, energy, water, and margin using the same model used in the live walk.

The real-site map presents terrain at footpath scale. It combines HiRISE 25 cm images, slope and elevation from the 1-meter HiRISE elevation model carried by Perseverance, CRISM carbonate mineral layer, and the path taken by Perseverance. Plan a route by clicking and it will be measured on the actual terrain. The default scientific loop turns up at 6.39 km in distance, climbs +133 meters and reaches 19 degrees in elevation.

2. Walk it: You will be guiding astronaut Jack in 3D (or use the auto-traverse to walk through the plan) using MERV, a six-wheeled rover buddy with a true rocker-bogie system. During each stop, you conduct the actual field procedure: abrasion, observation, sampling, documentation. The sequence is completed with the NASA picture of the task performed on Mars.

3. Survive whatever Mars gives you:

- Dust storms block out the light, the view and the power, but your balance stays. The density is 1% that of the Earth, making a 22 m/s wind feel like 2.4 m/s to walk into.

- Solar radiation events will hit you with protons that the suit does not shield but the lander cabin does. These are scaled to the most extreme event measured by Curiosity’s RAD (8.1 mGy, May 2024). The dose outside during the whole event is around 10 mSv. Inside, it is around 1 mSv. The background radiation dose uses RAD’s measurement of 0.64 mSv per sol.

- Earth is 11 light-minutes away, calculated dynamically based on true planetary orbits. Guidance is sent late, and completed experiments go back through relay orbiters. The model will suggest to shelter or abort, and ultimately it is up to you to decide.

- Debrief: See the science recovered, the samples sealed, the reserve kept, the radiation dose taken, and what the run taught you.

Use of Real NASA data:

  • MRO HiRISE: 25 cm imagery, live from NASA Mars Trek, and the 1 m elevation model of Jezero (USGS, Fergason et al. 2020), read straight from the source archive
  • MRO CRISM: carbonate map, observation FRT00005C5E, placed using the projection in its PDS label
  • Mars 2020 Perseverance: its real traverse, geology, Mastcam-Z and WATSON photographs, and MEDA weather ranges
  • Curiosity RAD: the surface radiation environment (Hassler et al. 2014)
  • JPL and NASA GISS Mars24: live Earth–Mars light time, Mars season, local solar time and sun angle
  • MOLA, CTX, THEMIS and Viking: regional context via Mars Trek

MERV, an interactive rover:

If you ask MERV about Mars, he will give you an answer based on facts from his handwritten knowledge database where all the information is referenced. If you ask him something about your hike ("Can I continue walking?", "How far is it to my home?"), then he will figure it out using the existing simulation. He will warn you that he will say "I don't know" in case he doesn't know anything. This behavior is unit-tested.

Benefits and impact:

  • To the students and public: experience the cost in terms of supplies, environment, conditions, and lag that walking on the human Marswalk would require.
  • To educators: a legible Mars Survival Guide that doesn’t require playing, and a two minute demo for the class.
  • To anyone considering manned missions to Mars: brings the difference between orbital observations and a safe first step into the light where it belongs. Crimson Exodus is a communication and training prototype that clearly states that it is not an operational route planner.

What makes it creative:

  1. Data from NASA becomes game play: real map alters your course, and real measurements determine your hazards.
  2. Light-time delay is the central game mechanic: It is the one rule that differentiates Mars from the Moon.
  3. Real images as the prize: Each activity concludes with a NASA image of the actual thing.
  4. Two-person cooperation mode and a mission control function; this way a classroom can do an EVA together.

Languages and hardware:

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML/CSS
  • Frontend: React 18, Three.js via React Three Fiber and drei (3D), Zustand (state management), Vite (building)
  • Multiplayer component: Node.js WebSocket server
  • Voice chat (optional): Web Speech API of the browser by default, Deepgram as an alternative
  • Deployment: GitHub Pages for app deployment and Render for multiplayer
  • Hardware: any laptop/desktop computer with a web browser. Quality of graphics varies depending on the computer.

What was considered by our group:

  • Data integrity: The model output is not presented as data, and the generated 3D landscape is clearly indicated as such.
  • Security: A statement indicating that this is just a demo and not an actual EVA planning tool.
  • Usability: No installation, no login required, controls on-screen, mobile optimization, and playability with the keyboard.
  • Efficiency: Fixed-timestep simulation with smooth visualization on regular laptops.
  • Privacy and security: No API keys stored in the browser and no voice ever leaving the computer.
  • Rights: NASA photos are cited on the photo, open-source fonts and libraries are used, and no AI-generated images are present.
